transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Doctor, I guess the main thing is I’m getting worried about how much I’m forgetting day to day. Not little things like where I put my glasses—though that happens too—but things I really shouldn’t be missing. Like I’ll have a heart follow-up appointment, and somehow it slips right past me, or the clinic calls and I’m supposed to call them back and then I don’t, even though I meant to.

And it’s embarrassing, honestly. I’ve also shown up to do a repair job and then realized I didn’t bring the right tools, the tools I knew I needed before I left. It’s like I know these things matter, and I tell myself I’m going to handle them, but then something gets lost between thinking it and actually doing it. That’s what brought me in.
Would you say this kind of forgetfulness and difficulty following through on tasks is something new for you, or has it been a pattern going back to your childhood or young adulthood?

No, I wouldn’t say it’s brand-new. Looking back, I think there’s been a pattern for a long time—probably since I was a kid, really. In grade school, I was always the boy who couldn’t seem to stay in his seat. The teacher would tell us to sit quietly, and I’d be half-standing or turning around or getting up for some reason.

And I remember blurting out answers before I was supposed to, even when I knew I should raise my hand. I wasn’t trying to be rude, I just… the answer would pop into my head and come out of my mouth. I also got notes sent home for talking too much. That happened more than once. So, no, it’s not like I suddenly became this way at 68. The forgetting feels more noticeable now, but the not slowing down and not always following the rules of the moment—that goes way back.
Over the past year or two, would you say your forgetfulness and trouble following through on tasks have been getting noticeably worse, or has it stayed about the same as it's always been?

I’d say it’s been noticeably worse in the sense that it’s been causing real trouble for, oh, maybe a year and a couple months now. Not my whole personality changing or anything, but the forgetfulness and not following through has started to matter more.

It seemed to really stand out after my cardiac scare, because I had to cut back on the walking and little projects that used to keep me kind of settled and moving in a routine. Before that, I could sort of burn off energy or keep myself on track by staying busy. Once I couldn’t do as much of that, things started slipping more. So I’d put it at about a year and two months where it’s been more of a problem day to day, not just “oh, I’ve always been like this.”
When you miss something like that follow-up appointment, if someone reminds you about it afterward, does it come back to you right away, or do you have no memory of it at all even when told?

Usually it comes back to me once they remind me, yes. Like if the clinic says, “You missed your heart follow-up,” I’ll think, “Oh, that was today?” or “That was yesterday?” and then I remember that I had known about it and meant to go. It’s not like the appointment never existed in my mind at all.

Same with calling the clinic back—I’ll remember when someone mentions it, and then I feel bad because I really did intend to do it. Or with the repair jobs, if I get there and don’t have the right tools, I know right away, “I knew I needed that.” It’s more like it slips out of reach at the time I’m supposed to act on it, not that I have no memory of it ever being planned.
Aside from forgetting to follow through on tasks, have you noticed any new difficulty learning new information, getting confused about where you are, or repeating yourself in conversations?

I don’t think so, no. At least not that I’ve noticed in a clear way. I mean, I can learn something new if someone shows me—maybe I need to pay attention and not get sidetracked, but I don’t feel like I can’t take in new information.

I haven’t been getting lost or confused about where I am, nothing like that. And as far as repeating myself, I suppose everybody repeats a story now and then, especially at my age, but I haven’t had people telling me, “You already said that three times,” or anything that stands out to me.

It feels more like I fail to do the thing at the right time, not that I don’t know what’s going on or can’t understand new things.
